Synonyms.title: Synonyms
Synonyms.weight: About 13 to 15 of the 60 Verbal Skills questions
Synonyms.oneLine: You are given one word and you pick the choice that comes closest to its meaning.

blocks.text: A synonym question is one word and four choices. You pick the choice nearest in meaning. Not a perfect match, just closer than the other three. About 13 to 15 of the 60 Verbal Skills questions work this way, which makes it one of the two most common types in the section.

This is a recognition test, not a thinking test. Either you know the word, in which case you should answer in about five seconds and bank the time, or you do not, in which case you need a method. There is very little in between that is worth 16 seconds.

The words themselves are not exotic. They are the words of middle-school reading, a step or two above everyday conversation. If you read books, you have already met most of them, even if you have never stopped to define them.
The method

items: Read the word and say what it means in your own words, before you look down at the choices. This keeps the choices from steering you.
Scan for the choice that matches what you said. If one clearly does, mark it and go.
If nothing matches, decide whether the word is positive or negative and cross out every choice with the wrong charge.
Break the word into its pieces — prefix, root, suffix — and see how much meaning falls out.
Answer, even if you are guessing. There is no penalty for a wrong answer on the HSPT, so a blank bubble is a wasted question.

blocks.text: Taking a word apart

Most long words are built out of smaller pieces, and the pieces carry meaning. Benevolent is bene (good) plus vol (wish): wishing good. Retract is re (back) plus tract (pull): to pull back. Inaudible is in (not) plus aud (hear): not able to be heard. You are not trying to rebuild the dictionary definition. You are trying to get close enough to tell four choices apart, and that is a much lower bar.
These are the pieces that pay off most often on this test.
Roots sit in the middle of the word and carry most of its meaning. A root you recognize can rescue a word you have never seen.

Suffixes rarely change what a word is about, but they tell you what kind of word it is, and that is worth knowing: the four choices are almost always the same part of speech as the word in the question. If the word ends in -ous, it is an adjective, and the answer will be an adjective too.
Positive or negative

When the pieces do not get you there, fall back on charge. Ask one question: does this word sound like a compliment or an insult, a good thing or a bad thing? You can often answer that even when you cannot define the word, because you have heard it used and you remember the tone of the sentence it was in. Then cross out every choice with the wrong charge. Sometimes only one choice survives, and you have answered the question without ever knowing exactly what the word means.

The four choices are almost always the same part of speech and all sound like real, plausible words. What separates them is direction and degree. Get the direction right — positive or negative, more or less — and you have usually cut four choices down to one or two.
Worked examples

blocks.stem: An abundant harvest is:
blocks.walkthrough: Say the meaning first: an abundant harvest is a big one, lots of it. That points straight at plentiful. The trap is scarce, which is on exactly the right topic — quantity — but points the wrong way. On synonym questions the opposite of the word is one of the most common wrong answers, because being about the right subject feels like being right.

blocks.stem: A benevolent ruler is:
blocks.walkthrough: If the word is not familiar, take it apart: bene means good and vol means wish, so a benevolent ruler wishes people well. Kindly is the only choice that says that. Cruel is the reversal trap and wealthy is an association — rulers are often rich, but the word does not mean rich.

blocks.stem: A credulous shopper is:
blocks.walkthrough: The root cred means believe, so the word has to do with believing, and the four choices force you to decide who is doing the believing. A credulous shopper believes whatever she is told, so she is trusting. Believable is the trap, and it is a good one: it means credible, which describes the thing being believed rather than the person doing it. Same root, opposite side of the sentence.

blocks.stem: A deleterious habit is:
blocks.walkthrough: There is no root here that most students will know, so use charge. You have probably only ever heard this word in a phrase like the deleterious effects of something, and that phrase is never good news, so the word is negative. Of the four choices only harmful is negative, and you are done without a definition. Delightful and delayed are there because they start with the same three letters, which is not a reason.

blocks.text: The traps

items: The opposite. The antonym of the word appears as a choice very often. It is about the right topic, so it feels related, and related is not the same as equal.
The look-alike. A choice that shares letters or a sound with the word but no meaning. Prudent and rude. Deleterious and delayed. Sound is not evidence.
The word-form shift. Credulous and credible, respectful and respectable. Same root, different jobs.
The right idea at the wrong strength. Warm is not scalding and annoyed is not furious. When two choices point the same way, the question is asking which degree matches.
The association. A word that turns up near the word in real life without meaning the same thing. A vessel is not a sailor.

blocks.text: When you are stuck

items: Put the word in a sentence you have actually heard or read. The sentence usually remembers the meaning even when you do not.
Decide the charge and cut every choice on the wrong side.

Look for two choices that mean roughly the same thing as each other. Only one answer can be correct, so if two choices are synonyms of each other, neither one is the answer. That can turn four choices into two.
Take the best of what is left, mark it and move. Two choices out of four is a real improvement over four, and guessing costs you nothing.
Do not go back and reread. Rereading a word you do not know does not make you know it, and it costs you a question elsewhere.

blocks.text: Worth memorizing

The three tables above. Roughly 20 prefixes and 20 roots cover a surprising share of the hard words on this test, and they keep paying you back in Reading and in Language too. Five a day for a month and you will meet them again on test day. Beyond that, the only reliable way to raise a vocabulary score is to read something every day that is a little harder than you find comfortable.

Antonyms.title: Antonyms
Antonyms.weight: About nine of the 60 Verbal Skills questions
Antonyms.oneLine: You are given one word and you pick the choice that means most nearly the opposite.

blocks.text: An antonym question looks almost exactly like a synonym question: one word, four choices. The difference is one word buried in the instruction — opposite. About nine of the 60 Verbal Skills questions are antonyms, and they are usually phrased as X means the opposite of.
It is the same skill as synonyms with the direction reversed, plus one trap that costs students more points than anything else in this part of the section.

A synonym of the word is planted among the four choices, nearly every time. It is there because it is the answer your eye wants. You read timid, you see shy, the two words light up together and your hand moves before your brain does. Before you mark anything, say the whole sentence in your head: the opposite of timid is ___. The word opposite in the middle is what saves you.
The method

items: Notice that this is an antonym question. Some students underline the word opposite every time. It looks unnecessary until the day you are tired and it is not.
Say what the word means, in your own words.
Say the opposite out loud in your head before you look at the choices. Now you are looking for something specific instead of shopping.
Find the choice closest to what you said.
Check the charge — whether the word is a good thing or a bad thing. If the word was negative and your answer is also negative, stop. You have almost certainly picked the planted synonym.

blocks.text: Charge does more work here than anywhere else

On a synonym question the answer has the same charge as the word, so charge cannot separate the answer from the sympathetic wrong choices. On an antonym question the answer has the opposite charge, which means charge alone eliminates. If the word is clearly negative, cross out every negative choice on sight. What is left is usually one word, occasionally two.

That single move handles a large share of these questions. Insolent is negative, so the answer is a positive word, and any choice that sounds like an insult is out no matter how well it fits the topic.
Prefixes that flip a word

A handful of prefixes exist only to reverse meaning. Sometimes the test hands you the answer this way: the opposite of audible is inaudible. More often it does not, but knowing them helps you read the choices quickly.
Worked examples

blocks.stem: Timid means the opposite of:
blocks.walkthrough: A timid person is easily frightened, so the opposite is someone unafraid: bold. Two of the four choices, shy and fearful, are synonyms of the word rather than opposites, and they are there for the student who reads the word and grabs. Polite is an association — timid people often seem polite — but politeness is not the reverse of fear.

blocks.stem: Abandon means the opposite of:
blocks.walkthrough: To abandon something is to leave it for good, so the opposite is to keep it: retain. Desert is the planted synonym and it is the most tempting choice on the list, because it is the closest word in meaning to the one in the question. On an antonym item, the choice that feels most closely connected is the one to check hardest.

blocks.stem: Augment means the opposite of:
blocks.walkthrough: To augment is to add to something, so the opposite is reduce. Two different traps are in play. Argue is a look-alike — augment and argument share letters and nothing else. Enlarge is the planted synonym, and it is the choice most students who half-know the word land on, because they recognize the meaning and forget the direction.

blocks.stem: Obstinate means the opposite of:
blocks.walkthrough: Start with charge: obstinate is a criticism, so the answer is a positive or neutral word, which removes hostile and noisy immediately. Between the two survivors, stubborn is what obstinate means and yielding is its reverse. Charge cuts the list in half and the synonym check finishes the job.

blocks.stem: Miserly means the opposite of:
blocks.walkthrough: A miserly person hoards money and will not spend it, so the opposite is generous. All three wrong choices are a different flavor of trap: stingy is the planted synonym, unhappy is a look-alike borrowed from miserable, and wealthy is an association, since misers in stories are usually rich. None of them is a reversal, and reversal is the only thing being asked for.

blocks.text: The traps

items: The planted synonym. Say it again: the word that means the same thing is almost always sitting right there. Assume it is until you have proved otherwise.
The look-alike. Miserly and miserable. Augment and argue. Shared letters are not shared meaning.
The association. A word that shows up alongside the word in real life. A miser is often wealthy, but wealthy is not the opposite of miserly.

The opposite of the other meaning. Some words have two senses. Blunt can be dull or it can be painfully direct, and those two senses have different opposites. Pick the sense the choices are built around.
The half-opposite. When two choices both point the other way, take the stronger one. Cool reverses hot a little; cold reverses it properly.

blocks.text: When you are stuck

items: Decide the charge of the word and cross out every choice on the same side. This is the highest-value three seconds you can spend on this question type.
Check the part of speech. The answer is almost always the same kind of word as the one in the question; a choice that is a noun when the word is an adjective is usually decoration.
If two choices mean nearly the same thing as each other, neither is the answer. Only one choice can be correct, so a matched pair is a matched pair of wrong answers.
Guess from what is left and move on. Nothing is subtracted for a wrong answer, and a 16-minute section does not forgive a 45-second question.

blocks.text: Worth memorizing

Nothing new. The same prefixes, roots and suffixes from the synonyms lesson do the work here, plus one habit worth drilling until it is automatic: on every antonym item, say the sentence the opposite of ___ is ___ before your pencil touches the page. The whole question type is built on students not doing that.

Analogies.title: Verbal Analogies
Analogies.weight: About 10 of the 60 Verbal Skills questions
Analogies.oneLine: You are given a pair of words and you pick the word that gives a second pair the same relationship.

blocks.text: An analogy reads A is to B as C is to ___, with four choices for the blank. About 10 of the 60 Verbal Skills questions are analogies.

The words are usually easy. The question is not testing whether you know them, it is testing whether you can see how two of them are connected and then find the same connection somewhere else. That is why an analogy can be missed by a student with an excellent vocabulary and answered instantly by one who has learned the method.
The method

items: Make a sentence out of the first pair that states the connection exactly. A broom is used to sweep.
Name the relationship if you can — purpose, part to whole, opposite and so on. Naming it is what makes the next step fast.
Put the third word into the same sentence and try each choice in the blank.
Keep the order. If your sentence is a rung is part of a ladder, the answer must be the whole, not another part.
Match the part of speech. If the first pair runs noun to adjective, the answer is an adjective.
If two choices still fit, your sentence is too loose. Make it narrower and run them again.

blocks.text: That last point is the one to take seriously. A dog is related to a bone is true of nearly any pair of words you could name, so it eliminates nothing. A dog chews a bone excludes almost everything. The looser your sentence, the more choices survive, and surviving choices are how you lose the question.

Say the relationship as a complete sentence before you read the choices. Everything else in this lesson is detail. Students who look straight at the four choices end up picking whichever word feels connected to the third word, and feels connected is exactly the material the wrong answers are built from.
The relationship categories

The people who write this test work from a list of relationship types, and the answer keys name them. Learning the list is worth doing, because recognizing the category tells you the shape of the answer before you have read a single choice.

head: Category
Example pair
The sentence you would say
rows: A broom is used to sweep.
A rung is part of a ladder.
To ascend is the opposite of to descend.
A needle is used together with thread.
An otter lives in a river.
A sonnet is a kind of poem.
Granite and marble are both stone.

blocks.text: Order and part of speech

Direction is half of the relationship. Wool is to sheep is product first, source second. If you build the sentence backwards you will happily pick a word that is wrong in a way you never notice, because the pair does have the right relationship — pointing the wrong way. Read your sentence back with the third word in it and check that it still sounds like the first one.

Part of speech is the fastest elimination available on this question type and it takes no thought at all. If the first pair is a noun and then an adjective, any choice that is not an adjective is out. That alone often removes two of the four.
Worked examples

blocks.stem: Scissors is to cut as broom is to:
blocks.walkthrough: The sentence is scissors are used to cut — object to purpose — so the answer has to be what a broom is used to do. Sweep is the only verb on the list, so part of speech settles it before meaning does. Floor and dustpan are things a broom is used near, and handle is a part of one; none of the three is a purpose.

blocks.stem: Rung is to ladder as page is to:
blocks.walkthrough: The sentence is a rung is part of a ladder, so the answer is the thing a page is part of: a book. Each wrong choice is a different relationship wearing the same clothes. Paper is what a page is made of, ink is what is on it and reading is what it is for. All true, none of them part to whole.

blocks.stem: Wool is to sheep as honey is to:
blocks.walkthrough: The sentence is wool comes from a sheep, so the answer is what honey comes from: a bee. This item is really a test of order. Hive is where the bee lives, and if you had built the sentence backwards as a sheep produces wool in a barn you would find yourself reaching for it. Sweet is a characteristic and jar is a container.

blocks.stem: Feather is to light as anvil is to:
blocks.walkthrough: A feather is light — object to characteristic, and light is an adjective, so the answer is an adjective. That removes iron, blacksmith and metal in one pass without your having to think about anvils at all. Heavy is left, and it is right: an anvil is heavy in the same obvious way a feather is light.

blocks.stem: Odometer is to distance as barometer is to:
blocks.walkthrough: The sentence is an odometer measures distance, which is measurement to range, so the answer must be the exact quantity a barometer measures. That is air pressure. Weather and forecast are what the reading gets used for, which is close enough to feel right and not close enough to be right, and temperature belongs to a different instrument. When a choice is in the right subject but not the exact quantity, tighten the sentence and it falls out.

blocks.text: The traps

items: The association. A word that goes with the third word in daily life. Bees make honey, so hive and flower both feel plausible on any bee question. Feeling connected is not a relationship.
The same-topic word. Ladders, rungs, steps, climbing — all one subject, only one of them in the right role.
The reversed pair. The right relationship pointing the wrong way. The only defense is reading your sentence back.
The material. Page and paper, door and wood. What a thing is made of is its own category and it is rarely the one being asked about.
The wrong part of speech. Nearly free to spot and it is on almost every analogy item.

blocks.text: When you are stuck

items: If one word in the first pair is unfamiliar, build the sentence out of what you do know. Often the four choices tell you the category on their own — if three of them are verbs, you are being asked about purpose.
Eliminate by part of speech first. It is mechanical, it is fast and it does not require you to have understood the question.
Cross out any choice that only connects to the third word by subject matter.
If two survive, add one more word to your sentence to make it stricter, then take the better one and move.
Guess and go. Nothing is deducted for a wrong answer, and this section does not give you the time to admire a hard question.

blocks.text: Worth memorizing

The category table. Twelve relationship names is a short list, and having the names in your head changes what you see when you read a pair. Instead of two words with a vague link you see part to whole, and the answer stops being a matter of taste. Practice by naming the category out loud on every analogy you do for a week, even the ones you get right instantly.

Classification.title: Verbal Classification
Classification.weight: About 16 of the 60 Verbal Skills questions — the largest single type
Classification.oneLine: You are given four words and you pick the one that does not belong with the other three.

blocks.text: Four words. Three of them belong together and one does not, and you pick the one that does not. About 16 of the 60 Verbal Skills questions are classifications, which makes this the single most common question type in the section — more common than synonyms, and worth more than a quarter of the whole Verbal score.

The words are not always nouns. You will see sets of verbs, sets of adjectives, sets of places and occasionally sets of proper names. The subject changes; the task never does. Find what three of them share.
The method

items: Read all four before you decide anything. The odd one is defined by the other three, so you cannot judge any word until you have seen the group.
Name the category that covers three of them, in words, in your head. Not a feeling — an actual phrase: three of these are instruments you blow into.
Test the fourth word against that phrase. If it fails the phrase, it is your answer.
If your phrase covers all four, or only covers two, it is the wrong phrase. Try another one.
Mark it and move. These should be your fastest questions in the section.

blocks.text: Name the category before you look for the odd one. Finish the sentence three of these are ___ out loud in your head. If you cannot finish it, you have not found the split yet, and a word that merely feels different is not a reason to choose it.
The right category leaves exactly one word out

This is the test of whether you have found the real split, and it settles more questions than anything else in this lesson. A correct category name includes three words and excludes one. If your name excludes two, it is not the name the question was built on, no matter how true it is.

Take square, triangle, circle and rectangle. Four-sided figures is a real category and it is no use here: it keeps the square and the rectangle and throws out the triangle and the circle, two on each side. Shapes made of straight lines keeps the square, the triangle and the rectangle and throws out the circle by itself. The second name is the one the question is built on. Count what your category leaves out before you commit to it.
Do not stop at the first plausible split

The first difference you notice is often a real difference and still not the answer. In sprint, jog, stroll and swim, the first thing most students see is that strolling is the slow one while the others are quick. That is true, and it is not the split: sprinting, jogging and strolling are all ways of moving on your own two feet, and swimming is not. Speed is a difference among the words. Being done on foot is the line that separates three from one.

As a rule of thumb: splits by degree — louder, bigger, faster, more expensive — are usually decoys, because degree is a sliding scale and the test wants a clean line. Splits by kind — this one is a different sort of thing from the other three — are usually the answer. When you find a degree split, spend one more second looking for a kind split underneath it.
When two readings both work

Some items genuinely support two answers, and this is where most legitimate complaints about this question type come from. Two rules keep you out of trouble. First, prefer the category based on what the things are over one based on where they are found or what they are sometimes used for; a category built on an unusual fact you happen to know is almost never the intended one. Second, prefer the plainer name — the one a seventh grader would say first. The test is not trying to be clever with you.

If you are still split after ten seconds, take the more obvious of the two, mark it and go. An ambiguous classification item is worth exactly one point, the same as every other question in the section, and it is not worth the three questions you could answer with the time you would spend arguing with it.
Worked examples

blocks.stem: Which word does not belong with the others?
blocks.walkthrough: All four are musical instruments, so that category is too big to be the split — it leaves nobody out. Go one level finer: the violin, the cello and the harp all make their sound from strings, and the trumpet is blown. Three strings, one horn. Whenever all four words share an obvious category, the split you want is one level below the label you thought of first.

blocks.stem: Which word does not belong with the others?
blocks.walkthrough: Two tempting names both fail the counting test: has an engine keeps the motorcycle and the car and drops two, and powered by a person keeps the canoe and the bicycle and drops two. Runs on wheels keeps the bicycle, the motorcycle and the car and drops the canoe alone, so that is the split. When a category leaves two words out, it is not the one the question was written around, however true it is.

blocks.stem: Which word does not belong with the others?
blocks.walkthrough: The tempting split is volume: shouting is loud and the other two are quiet, so shout looks like the outlier. That is a split by degree and it is a decoy. Whispering, shouting and murmuring are all ways of using your voice, while listening is something you do with your ears — a split by kind, and the one that holds.

blocks.stem: Which word does not belong with the others?
blocks.walkthrough: Name the category first: three of these are garden tools. A shovel, a rake and a hoe are all things you hold; a harvest is the work you do with them, or its result. Every word in the set belongs to the same scene, which is the point — a set can be all on one topic and still have a clean line through it. Do not look for the word that feels out of place, look for the word that fails the phrase.

blocks.stem: Which word does not belong with the others?
blocks.walkthrough: Sentences, paragraphs and chapters are all parts of a written work, arranged small to large. A novel is the whole work, not a piece of one. The trap is looking for the extreme — students often reach for sentence as the smallest or novel as the longest and pick on size rather than role. Size is degree. Part against whole is kind.

blocks.text: The traps

items: Degree instead of kind. The loudest, the biggest or the most expensive word looks like an outlier and usually is not.
Stopping at the obvious category. When all four words fit one label, the split is a level finer than the label you first thought of.

The unfamiliar word. If three words form a clean category, the fourth is the answer even if you cannot define it. But if only two of them group, the strange word is not automatically the odd one — that is a guess dressed up as reasoning.
Mixed parts of speech. Occasionally the split is grammatical: three verbs and a noun. Worth a glance when the meanings will not separate.
Overthinking. The clever category you constructed is almost never the intended one. Plain beats ingenious on this question type.

blocks.text: When you are stuck

items: Write, or at least say, two candidate category names.
Ask of each one: how many words does it leave out? Keep the one that leaves exactly one.
If both leave exactly one, take the plainer name — the one about what the things are rather than what they are used for or where they turn up.
Still stuck after ten seconds? Guess and move. Nothing is subtracted for a wrong answer, and with 16 seconds a question you cannot afford to buy a hard item with the time for three easy ones.

blocks.text: Worth memorizing

Nothing, and that is the good news about this question type: there is no list to learn. What improves is speed, and speed comes from doing enough of them that naming the category becomes automatic. Since classifications are the largest block of questions in Verbal Skills and they carry no vocabulary requirement beyond what you already have, they are the most efficient practice on this section. Do 20 a day and time yourself.

Verbal Logic.title: Verbal Logic
Verbal Logic.weight: About 10 to 12 of the 60 Verbal Skills questions
Verbal Logic.oneLine: You are given three statements and you decide whether the third one is true, false or uncertain if the first two are true.

blocks.text: Three short statements. You are told to assume the first two are true, and you decide whether the third is true, false or uncertain. About 10 to 12 of the 60 Verbal Skills questions are built this way.

This is the only question type in Verbal Skills that does not depend on vocabulary at all, which makes it the best place on the section to gain points. It runs on one rule. Learn the rule properly and these become the questions you finish fastest and miss least.

The third statement is false only if the first two make it impossible. If the first two simply do not settle the matter, the answer is uncertain — even when you know from the outside world that the statement is wrong.
The three verdicts

items: True — the first two statements force it. There is no way for both of them to be true and the third one false.
False — the first two statements forbid it. There is no way for both of them to be true and the third one true as well.
Uncertain — the first two allow it without requiring it. It might be true, it might not, and the statements do not say.

blocks.text: Look closely at what uncertain means, because it is the verdict students misunderstand. It does not mean probably not. It does not mean the statements are about something else. It means the first two statements leave the question open. Most students use this answer far less often than they should, and every unused uncertain is a point.
Why a statement you know is wrong can still be uncertain

You are not being asked whether the third statement is true in the world. You are being asked what follows from the first two statements and nothing else. Pretend you know nothing except what those two sentences told you, and answer from there.

Take these three: All penguins are birds. A robin is a bird. A robin is a penguin. You know perfectly well that a robin is not a penguin. But look at what you were given. The first statement says penguins are inside the group called birds. The second says robins are inside that group too. Neither statement says the two kinds cannot overlap, so nothing you were told rules the third statement out. It is not proven, and it is not forbidden. The answer is uncertain, and the fact that you happen to know a robin from a penguin is information the question did not give you and does not want.
That feels wrong the first few times. It stops feeling wrong once you accept what the question is actually asking, which is not is this true? but did the first two statements settle this?
A procedure you can run in 15 seconds

items: Decide which kind of item it is. Comparisons use words like taller, faster, older, more than, as many as. Categories use all, every, some, no, none.
For a comparison, put the names in a single line, largest on the left, using only what the statements actually say.
Read the third statement against the line. Agrees with the line: true. Reverses the line: false. Names never connected to each other: uncertain.

For a category item, ask whether the second statement puts its subject inside the group the first statement talks about. Inside means you get a definite answer. Merely sharing a trait with that group means uncertain.
Before you mark false, make sure the first two make the third impossible, not just unproven. Unproven is uncertain.

blocks.text: Comparison chains

Comparisons are the friendliest items here, because a definite answer is usually available. The whole technique is to draw the line. Do not hold three relationships in your head under time pressure; put the names in order in the margin, biggest first, and read the answer off.
A three-term chain links everything: if A is above B and B is above C, then A is above C. This is the pattern that produces most of the true answers on this question type.

blocks.stem: Maya's backpack is heavier than Devon's. Devon's backpack is heavier than Ruth's. Maya's backpack is heavier than Ruth's.
blocks.walkthrough: Write the line heaviest first: Maya, Devon, Ruth. Every name is connected to the next one, so the whole line is fixed and Maya is above Ruth on it. The third statement agrees with the line, so it is true. Chains like this are the closest thing to free points in Verbal Skills.

blocks.text: Four-term chains work the same way and are only longer. The extra name is often there to make you lose track, not to complicate the logic.

blocks.stem: Priya finished ahead of Malik, and Malik finished ahead of Cole. Cole finished ahead of Sana. Priya finished ahead of Sana.
blocks.walkthrough: The first statement gives you two links at once. The line reads Priya, Malik, Cole, Sana, first to last, and every neighbor is connected, so the order of all four is settled. Priya is ahead of Sana on that line, so the third statement is true. Notice that the first statement carried two relationships; count links, not sentences.

blocks.text: A chain only settles a comparison if the two names in the third statement actually end up connected. When two names are each compared to a third but never to each other, the line has a fork in it and no definite answer exists.

blocks.stem: Rosa runs faster than Kim. Tomas runs faster than Kim. Rosa runs faster than Tomas.
blocks.walkthrough: Both statements compare somebody to Kim, and neither compares Rosa with Tomas. All you know is that Kim is slower than both of them; above Kim the order could go either way. The answer is uncertain. This is the shape to watch for: when the same name appears in both of the first two statements as the smaller side, the other two names are usually left unconnected.

blocks.text: Equality, and mixing more with as many as

As many as, as long as and the same as are equal signs. They do not make anything bigger; they pass a comparison straight through. If Ana has as many as Ben, then anything true about Ben's amount is true about Ana's, and the two of them sit at the same point on your line.

The trap is reading as many as as though it meant more than. It does not. It is exactly equal, which is precisely why it is useful: it lets you connect two names without changing the order of anything.

blocks.stem: The orchard has more apple trees than pear trees. It has as many plum trees as pear trees. The orchard has more apple trees than plum trees.
blocks.walkthrough: Plum equals pear, so put them at the same spot on the line, and apple is above pear. Since plum sits exactly where pear sits, apple is above plum too. True. The equal sign did all the work by moving the plum trees onto a name you already had placed.

blocks.stem: Ben scored higher than Cara. Dev scored higher than Cara. Dev scored the same as Ben.
blocks.walkthrough: Ben and Dev are both above Cara and nothing connects them to each other, so they could be equal or either one could be higher. The statements allow the third without requiring it, which is the definition of uncertain. Beware the reflex that says the same sounds like a strong claim and strong claims must be false — how a statement sounds is not evidence.

blocks.stem: The hall is longer than the gym. The gym is exactly as long as the cafeteria, and the library is longer than the cafeteria. The library is longer than the gym.
blocks.walkthrough: Ignore the hall; it is a spare part. The gym and the cafeteria are equal, so they occupy the same point on the line, and the library is above the cafeteria, which means it is above the gym as well. True. Four names, one of them irrelevant, and an equal sign in the middle — that is about as hard as a comparison item gets.

blocks.text: All, some and none

Categorical items use all, every, some and no. The key fact is that all is a one-way street. All A are B tells you that everything in group A is also in group B. It tells you nothing whatever about whether a particular thing in B is in A, because B is the bigger group and has room for other things.

Picture it as an arrow: all trumpets point into brass. You may travel along the arrow — find a trumpet, conclude it is brass — but never against it. Finding something brass tells you nothing about whether it is a trumpet.

Some means at least one, and no more than that. Some tools are rusty guarantees that at least one rusty tool exists; it does not promise that the rest are shiny, and it does not tell you which ones. No and none are the strongest of the four, because they forbid, and forbidding is what produces a verdict of false.
The undistributed middle

This one pattern costs students more points than anything else in Verbal Logic, so it is worth naming and learning cold. It looks like this: All A are B. C is B. Therefore C is A. The answer is uncertain, every single time.

Here is why. The first statement puts A inside B. The second puts C inside B as well. B is the larger circle and it contains things that are not A, so C might be one of those, or C might be an A. Nothing you were told decides it. The argument travels against the arrow, which the arrow does not allow — but failing to prove something is not the same as disproving it, so the verdict is uncertain rather than false.

blocks.stem: All the trumpets in the school band are made of brass. Nadia's instrument is made of brass. Nadia plays the trumpet.
blocks.walkthrough: This is the pattern exactly: all trumpets are brass, Nadia's instrument is brass, so Nadia plays a trumpet. But brass is the bigger group and a tuba is brass too. The statements do not rule the trumpet out and do not require it, so the answer is uncertain. Nothing said the band has only trumpets.

blocks.stem: All penguins are birds. A robin is a bird. A robin is a penguin.
blocks.walkthrough: Everything in you wants to answer false, because you know robins from penguins. Look only at what you were given: penguins are inside birds, robins are inside birds, and neither statement says the two cannot overlap. The first two do not make the third impossible, so it is uncertain. Outside knowledge is not evidence on this question type, and this item exists to find out whether you know that.

blocks.text: Compare a version that runs along the arrow instead of against it. Same words, different direction, definite answer.

blocks.stem: Every member of the chess club stayed after school on Friday. Jonah is a member of the chess club. Jonah stayed after school on Friday.
blocks.walkthrough: The second statement puts Jonah inside the group the first statement is about, so the first statement applies to him directly. This is travel along the arrow, and it produces a definite answer: true. The difference between this item and the one before it is only which way the second statement points, and that difference is the whole question type.

blocks.stem: Some of the tools in the shed are rusty. Every rusty tool in the shed is a saw. Some of the saws in the shed are rusty.
blocks.walkthrough: Some guarantees that at least one rusty tool exists. The second statement says every rusty tool in the shed is a saw, so that tool is a saw, and it is rusty. At least one rusty saw therefore exists, which is exactly what the third statement claims. True. With some items, find the thing the statement guarantees exists and follow it.

blocks.text: When the answer really is false

False is the rarest of the three verdicts, and it turns up in two recognizable shapes. The first is a comparison whose order the third statement reverses. The second is a flat contradiction of a no, none or every statement. In both, the first two statements do not merely fail to support the third — they rule it out.

blocks.stem: The blue house is older than the green house. The green house is older than the yellow house. The yellow house is older than the blue house.
blocks.walkthrough: The line reads blue, green, yellow, oldest to newest, and it is fully connected, so the position of all three is fixed. The third statement puts yellow above blue, which the line forbids. That is impossible rather than merely unproven, so the answer is false. Reversal of a settled order is the most common way a false answer is built.

blocks.stem: No student in Mr. Alvarez's class rides the bus. Elena is a student in Mr. Alvarez's class. Elena rides the bus.
blocks.walkthrough: The second statement puts Elena inside the group, and the first statement forbids everyone in that group from riding the bus. So the third statement is not just unsupported, it is impossible: false. Note the contrast with the trumpet item. There, the second statement only said that Nadia shared a trait with the group. Here it says Elena is in it.

blocks.text: Same structure, three different verdicts

head: Statements one and two
Statement three
Answer
Why
rows: Ivy is taller than Sam. Sam is taller than Noor.
The line reads Ivy, Sam, Noor. The third statement agrees with it.
Ivy is taller than Sam. Sam is taller than Noor.
The same line puts Noor last. The third statement reverses it, so the first two make it impossible.
Ivy is taller than Sam. Noor is taller than Sam.
Both are above Sam and nothing compares Ivy with Noor. The statements allow it without requiring it.

blocks.text: The three items differ by a handful of words. Two of them use the same third statement and have different answers, and one of them changes only which name sits on which side of the second statement. That is the level of attention these questions ask for, and it is why you read the second statement twice.
The traps

items: Answering from the world instead of from the statements. The most expensive habit on this question type, and the one the undistributed middle items are designed to catch.
Calling it false when it is only unproven. False means impossible. If you cannot show it is impossible, it is uncertain.
Traveling against the arrow. All A are B never tells you that a B is an A.
Reading as many as as more than. It is an equal sign. It moves a name onto the line without changing the order.
Missing the fork. When both of the first two statements compare somebody to the same person, check whether the two names in the third statement were ever compared to each other.
Swapping the names. The names are short, similar and deliberately easy to reverse when you are rushing. Read the third statement once more before you mark it.

blocks.text: If you cannot decide

Then the answer is uncertain, and that is not a guess, it is the definition. If you have read the first two statements with care and you can neither show that the third must be true nor show that it is impossible, uncertain is the correct answer, not the consolation prize. The mistake is the opposite one: sitting on an item hunting for a proof that is not there.

And if you are lost because the wording has tangled you up rather than the logic, mark uncertain and move on. There is no penalty for a wrong answer on the HSPT, and at 16 seconds a question the time is worth more than the item.
Worth memorizing

items: False means impossible. Unproven means uncertain.
All A are B travels one way only.
All A are B; C is B; therefore C is A is uncertain, always.
For comparisons, write the line, largest on the left.
As many as is an equal sign, not a bigger sign.
Two names that never got compared cannot produce a definite answer.

Number Series.title: Number Series
Number Series.weight: About 18 to 22 of the 52 Quantitative Skills questions — the largest type
Number Series.oneLine: A short run of numbers, letters or both follows a hidden rule, and you supply the term that is missing.

blocks.text: Series questions are the largest single block on the Quantitative Skills section. You are shown four to seven terms that follow a rule nobody tells you, and you supply a term that is missing. The terms may be whole numbers, fractions, decimals, letters, Roman numerals or a mix of these.

The rules are not clever. Almost every series on this test is built from adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing or stepping through the alphabet. What makes the questions hard is the clock. The section gives you 52 questions in 30 minutes, which is about 35 seconds each, and no calculator. Speed here comes from running the same procedure every time, not from being quick at arithmetic.
The method

items: Read the whole series before you write anything. Notice what kind of terms these are, and notice exactly where the blank sits.
Write the difference between each pair of neighboring terms in the gap between them. Do this even when you think you already see the pattern.
If the differences are all the same, the rule is add that number. You are done.
If the differences are not the same, take the differences of the differences. If those are constant, the series is progressive and the next gap is predictable.
If the terms climb or fall steeply, look for a ratio instead. Divide each term by the one before it.
If none of that works, stop treating the series as one chain. Read every other term. Two simple series braided together look like one complicated series.
Apply your rule to get the term the item asks for, then test the rule against a pair you have not used yet. A rule that explains only the front of the series is the wrong rule.

blocks.text: Before you answer, count which position the blank occupies. Items that put the blank in the middle, or at the very start, are the ones students miss — not because the rule is hard but because they compute the term after the blank instead of the blank itself. Once you have a candidate, drop it back into the series and read the whole thing forward.
Take the differences first
Take \(7, 12, 17, 22, 27\). Under the gaps write \(5, 5, 5, 5\). Constant, so add five and the next term is \(32\). That is most series questions, and it takes about eight seconds.

Now take \(5, 6, 9, 14, 21, 30\). The differences are \(1, 3, 5, 7, 9\), which are not constant — but the differences of those are \(2, 2, 2, 2\). The gap grows by two every step, so the next gap is \(11\) and the next term is \(41\). A series whose gaps grow by a fixed amount is called progressive, and taking a second round of differences is the only thing you need to crack it.

When a series climbs steeply the differences will never settle, so divide instead of subtracting. In \(3, 12, 48, 192\) each term is four times the one before it, and the next term is \(768\). Falling series work the same way. In \(405, 135, 45, 15\) each term is one third of the last, so the next is \(5\).
The families you will meet

Every series on the test is one of these shapes. Read the table once, then work through the examples below — recognizing the family is most of the battle, because once you name it the arithmetic is trivial.

blocks.text: Letter series

Letters are numbers in disguise. A is 1 and Z is 26. Write the position numbers under the letters and a letter series becomes a number series, which you already know how to solve. You do not need to recite the whole alphabet with its numbers; you need six anchors. A is 1, F is 6, K is 11, P is 16, U is 21, Z is 26. From an anchor you can count forward two or three letters faster than you can count from the beginning.

Two things to watch. First, a letter series can run past Z and wrap round to A, so treat the alphabet as a loop rather than a line. Second, when the terms are pairs or triples of letters, each position usually follows its own rule. Read all the first letters together, then all the second letters together, and do not try to see both at once.
When the repetition is the pattern

Some letter series carry their rule in how many times a letter is written rather than in which letter it is. In Q, RR, SSS, TTTT the letter advances by one and the number of copies advances by one, so the next term is UUUUU. Count the copies before you look at anything else; if the counts are \(1, 2, 3, 4\) you have found the rule and the letters will follow an easy pattern of their own.

Mixed strings work the same way. In B4, D8, F12, H16 the letters and the numbers are two separate series that happen to be printed next to each other. Solve them separately — letters ahead two, numbers up four — and put the answers back together as J20. The same applies when Roman numerals are mixed with Arabic ones: convert every Roman numeral to a plain number first, and the series usually turns out to be something ordinary like counting by two.
Where the blank sits

Four formats appear, and they are not equally easy. You may be asked for the next term, for the next two terms, for a blank in the middle of the series, or for the missing first term. The last two are where students lose points. With a medial blank, find the rule from the terms on both sides of the gap and then check that your answer works forwards and backwards. With an initial blank, you have to run the rule in reverse: if the series adds five going right, it subtracts five going left.
Numbers worth having ready

blocks.stem: Look at this series: 9, 16, 23, ___, 37, 44. What number should fill the blank?
blocks.walkthrough: Take the differences you can see: \(16-9=7\) and \(23-16=7\), and at the other end \(44-37=7\). The series adds seven. The blank is the fourth term, so it is \(23+7=30\), and the check works both ways because \(30+7=37\). The wrong choices are all near misses — they come from settling on a difference of five or six after glancing at only one pair, which is why you take at least two differences before committing.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: 4, 30, 8, 26, 12, 22, 16, ___. What number comes next?
blocks.walkthrough: The differences swing wildly — \(+26\), \(-22\), \(+18\) — which is the signal to stop reading it as one chain. Read the odd positions: 4, 8, 12, 16, going up by four. Read the even positions: 30, 26, 22, going down by four. The blank is the eighth term, an even position, so it continues 30, 26, 22 and the answer is 18. The trap is 20, which is what you get by carrying the odd chain forward from 16 without noticing which position you are filling.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: ___, PR, SU, VX, YA. What letter pair belongs in the blank at the beginning?
blocks.walkthrough: Treat the two positions separately. The first letters are P, S, V, Y — that is 16, 19, 22, 25, going up by three — so the missing first letter is \(16-3=13\), which is M. The second letters are R, U, X, A — 18, 21, 24, then a wrap round to 1 — also up by three, so the missing second letter is \(18-3=15\), which is O. The answer is MO. LN steps back four instead of three; NP steps back only two; MP gets the first letter right and then reuses the wrong gap inside the pair.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: 2, 8, 5, 20, 17, 68, ___. What number comes next?
blocks.walkthrough: The terms rise, fall, rise, fall, so two operations are alternating. Check them in order: \(2\times4=8\), \(8-3=5\), \(5\times4=20\), \(20-3=17\), \(17\times4=68\). The pattern is multiply by four, subtract three, repeating, and the step after \(\times 4\) is \(-3\), so the answer is \(68-3=65\). The trap is 272, which applies the operation you just used instead of the one that comes next; 71 reverses the sign of the subtraction.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: C3, F9, I27, L81, ___. What comes next?
blocks.walkthrough: Split the letters from the numbers. C, F, I, L are 3, 6, 9, 12, so the next letter is 15, which is O. The numbers 3, 9, 27, 81 have no constant difference but a constant ratio of three, so the next is \(81\times3=243\). Put them back together for O243. M243 advances the letter by one, P243 advances it by four and O162 doubles the number instead of tripling it — each wrong choice gets one of the two series right and the other wrong, which is exactly how these distractors are built.

blocks.text: The traps

items: A rule that fits only the front of the series. Two terms will agree with almost any rule. Test yours on the last pair as well as the first.
Answering with the term after the blank. On medial-blank and initial-blank items this is the most common single error, and the test always offers that term as a choice.
Reducing a fraction. In \(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{2}{4}, \frac{3}{8}, \frac{4}{16}\) the pattern lives in the unreduced numbers. Simplify \(\frac{2}{4}\) to \(\frac{1}{2}\) and the pattern vanishes.
Reading an interleaved series as one chain. If the differences alternate between large positive and large negative, you are looking at two series, not one.
Miscounting the alphabet. Under time pressure it is easy to slide one letter. Count from the nearest anchor, not from A.
Choices one step short or one step long. When a series is \(+6\) each time, the choices will include the term before and the term after the one you want. Recount the position.

blocks.text: When you are stuck

items: Give it 15 seconds of differences and ratios. If neither settles, check the odd and even positions. If that fails too, guess and move on — a series you cannot see in 30 seconds is not worth 90.
Work backward from the choices. Drop each option into the blank and read the series aloud in your head; the right one makes the whole line regular, and usually only one does.
Eliminate by size. If the series is climbing, any choice smaller than the term before the blank is out. If it is falling, any choice larger is out. That often leaves two.
Never leave a series blank. There is no penalty for a wrong answer on the HSPT, so an unanswered question is strictly worse than a guess.

blocks.text: Worth memorizing

items: The alphabet anchors: A is 1, F is 6, K is 11, P is 16, U is 21, Z is 26.
The squares up to \(15^2=225\) and the cubes up to \(10^3=1000\).
The procedure itself. Differences, then differences of differences, then ratios, then odd and even positions. Running it in that order without thinking is what buys you the time.

Letter Series.title: Letter Series
Letter Series.weight: About four of the 52 Quantitative Skills questions
Letter Series.oneLine: A run of letters, or of letters and numbers together, follows a rule you have to name before you can supply the missing term.

blocks.text: Four or five of the series items on a form are built from letters rather than numbers. The terms may be single letters, pairs like GT and HS, triples like MCF, groups that repeat a letter several times, or a letter tied to a number as in B5 and D9. The task never changes: name the rule, then supply the term the item asks for.

These questions are worth practicing separately from number series because the arithmetic is trivial and the bookkeeping is not. Almost nobody misses one of these because they cannot add two. They miss it because they counted the alphabet wrong, or moved one letter of a pair and forgot the other, or wrote the right two letters in the wrong order.
The method

items: Before the section starts, write the alphabet down the margin of your scratch paper with the position number beside every letter. You write it once and use it on every letter item on the form.
Read the whole series and count how many characters each term holds. One letter, two, three, a letter and a number — that count tells you how many rules you are looking for.
Look for a character that never changes. A letter appearing in the same position in every term is scenery; copy it straight into your answer and stop thinking about it.
Take each remaining position on its own. Write the position numbers under all the first letters, then under all the second letters, and find the step for each column separately.
Write your answer out character by character, in order, from those separate rules.
Check it against the term on the other side of the blank. If the item gives a term after the gap, your answer has to lead into it as well as follow from the term before it.

blocks.text: Two rules running at once is the normal case, not the hard case. In GT, HS, IR the first letter climbs and the second falls, and the only reliable way to see that is to handle the two columns one after the other. Trying to watch both at the same time is what produces answers like KQ, where one column is right and the other never moved.
Count positions, do not recite

Reciting the alphabet under time pressure is how you slide one letter, and one letter is always among the choices. Count instead. Six anchors are enough to place any letter quickly: A is 1, F is 6, K is 11, P is 16, U is 21 and Z is 26. To find the letter five past R, start from P at 16, so R is 18, and 18 plus 5 is 23, which is W. That is faster and steadier than singing through the alphabet from the beginning.

The alphabet is a loop on this test, not a line. A series that steps forward three from X does not stop at Z; it wraps round, so X, then A, then D. When a column of letters runs into the end of the alphabet, subtract 26 and keep going: 24 plus 3 is 27, and 27 minus 26 is 1, which is A.
The shapes you will meet

Every letter item on the test is one of the shapes below. Read the table once and then work the examples, because naming the shape is most of the work. Once you know that one letter is fixed and the others advance two, the answer takes about five seconds.
