blocks.text: A letter that stands still

In three-letter terms one position is often frozen. MCF, MEF, MGF holds the M and the F and moves only the middle letter. PDQ, PGT, PJW holds the P at the front and moves the other two. Find the frozen letter first, write it into the answer straight away and you have turned a three-letter problem into a one-letter or two-letter problem. The choices will include a term that moves the frozen letter as well, which is why it is worth naming it out loud before you go on.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: TBW, TDW, TFW, ___, TJW. What term is missing?
blocks.walkthrough: The first letter is T in every term and the last is W in every term, so both are scenery. That leaves the middle column: B, D, F, blank, J. In position numbers that reads \(2\), \(4\), \(6\), blank, \(10\), climbing by two, so the missing letter is \(8\), which is H. The answer is THW, and it checks forward because H to J is another step of two. TIW moves the middle letter only one; THX moves the last letter, which never moves; WHT is the right three letters written backward, and a reversed term is offered on nearly every item of this kind.

blocks.text: Two letters walking in opposite directions

The most common two-letter shape sends one letter up the alphabet and the other down. GT, HS, IR looks complicated until you split it: G, H, I is plus one, and T, S, R is minus one. Handle the columns in order, write the two answers down, then join them. The danger is that both columns are moving by one, so a term with the columns swapped still looks plausible at a glance.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: FU, GT, HS, IR, ___. What term comes next?
blocks.walkthrough: First column: F, G, H, I are \(6, 7, 8, 9\), so the next is \(10\), which is J. Second column: U, T, S, R are \(21, 20, 19, 18\), so the next is \(17\), which is Q. Join them for JQ. JR repeats the second letter instead of stepping it back, KQ pushes the first letter two, and QJ is your own answer written backward — the choice that catches students who solve the columns in the order they find them rather than the order they are printed.

blocks.text: When the repetition is the rule

Some series carry their pattern in how many times a letter is written. In R, QQ, P, OO, N the letters simply walk backward one at a time, and on top of that every second term is doubled. In K, L, K, LL, K, LLL, K a single K sits between groups of L that gain one letter each time, and the K is doing nothing at all except separating the groups. Count the copies before you look at the letters. If the counts run 1, 2, 3, 4 or alternate 1, 2, 1, 2, you have found half the rule already.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: S, RR, Q, PP, O, ___. What term comes next?
blocks.walkthrough: Read the letters alone: S, R, Q, P, O, which is \(19, 18, 17, 16, 15\), stepping back one, so the sixth letter is \(14\), which is N. Now read the counts alone: one, two, one, two, one, so the sixth term is doubled. Put the two rules together and the answer is NN. The choice N drops the doubling, NNN invents a count that never appears in the series, and MM skips a letter by counting the doubled terms as two steps instead of one.

blocks.text: A letter and a number at the same time

Mixed terms such as B5, D9, F13 or C3, F12, I48 are two separate series printed side by side. Cover the numbers with a finger and solve the letters; cover the letters and solve the numbers. The two rules do not have to be the same kind: in C3, F12, I48 the letters add three each time while the numbers multiply by four. Every wrong choice on an item like this gets one half right and the other half wrong, so both halves have to be checked.

Watch the order of the characters as well as their values. In 5J, K9, 5L, M9 the letters run J, K, L, M, N straight through and the numbers alternate 5 and 9, but the terms holding a 5 put the number first and the terms holding a 9 put it last. Getting the two characters right and printing them the wrong way round is a wrong answer, and it is always one of the four choices.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: D2, G6, J18, ___. What term comes next?
blocks.walkthrough: Split the terms. The letters D, G, J are \(4, 7, 10\), climbing by three, so the next letter is \(13\), which is M. The numbers 2, 6, 18 have no constant difference, but each is three times the one before it, so the next is \(18 \times 3 = 54\). The answer is M54. M24 adds six to the number instead of tripling it, L54 advances the letter only two, and N54 advances it four — three choices, each of which solves exactly one of the two strands.

blocks.text: When the blank comes first

An item that asks what term should come first is the same problem run backward. Find the rule from the terms you can see, then invert it: a column that adds four going right subtracts four going left, and a column that steps back one going right steps forward one going left. Students lose these by finding the rule correctly and then applying it in the direction they read, which lands them one term past the front of the series instead of one term before it.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: ___, HL, LP, PT, TX. What term should come first?
blocks.walkthrough: Both columns move the same way here. First letters H, L, P, T are \(8, 12, 16, 20\), jumping four, so the term before H is \(8 - 4 = 4\), which is D. Second letters L, P, T, X are \(12, 16, 20, 24\), also jumping four, so the letter before L is \(12 - 4 = 8\), which is H. The answer is DH. CG steps both letters back five, DL gets the first letter right and leaves the second where it was, and HD is DH reversed.

blocks.text: The traps

items: Reciting instead of counting. Slide one letter early in the alphabet and every letter after it is wrong. Count from the nearest anchor, and write the alphabet in the margin so you never have to recite at all.
The reversed term. XM for MX, PK for KP, FIM for MIF. Your own answer written backward is offered on nearly every letter item on the test. Read your letters left to right once more before you mark.
Moving one column and forgetting the other. Two letters means two rules. A choice that gets the first letter right and leaves the second unchanged is the single most common distractor here.
Missing a letter that never moves. If the same letter sits in the same position in every term, it belongs in your answer untouched. Choices that shift it look almost right.
Reading a mixed term as one rule. In C3, F12, I48 the letters add and the numbers multiply. Solve the strands separately or you will force one rule onto both.
Following the wrong strand. In K, L, K, LL, K, LLL the K is a separator, not part of the pattern. Continuing it gives K or KKKK, and both are offered.
Stopping at Z. The alphabet wraps. If a column runs past 26, subtract 26 and carry on from A.

blocks.text: When you are stuck

items: Number the letters. Write the position of every letter under it and the series usually turns into something like \(4, 7, 10\), which you can read at a glance.
Test the choices. Drop each one into the blank and read the whole series through. On letter items only one choice normally survives a reading in both directions.
Eliminate on direction. If a column is climbing, any choice that moves that letter backward is gone, and that often leaves two.
Guess and move on. There is no penalty for a wrong answer on the HSPT, so mark your best remaining choice. Four letter items are not worth four minutes.

blocks.text: Worth memorizing

items: The alphabet anchors: A is 1, F is 6, K is 11, P is 16, U is 21, Z is 26.
Z wraps round to A. Past 26, subtract 26.
Each position in a multi-character term has its own rule, and the rules can be of different kinds.
A frozen letter is scenery. Copy it and move on.
The habit that pays for itself: write the alphabet with its numbers in the margin before you answer the first question of the section.

Comparisons.title: Comparisons
Comparisons.weight: About 16 to 19 of the 52 questions, split between figure comparisons and expression comparisons
Comparisons.oneLine: Three labeled quantities or figures are given, and you choose the statement that correctly orders them.

blocks.text: A comparison item hands you three things labeled A, B and C and asks for the best answer. The four choices are not numbers — they are statements about how the three compare, built from \(=\), \(\lt\) and \(\gt\). Your job is to work out what A, B and C actually are and then find the statement that is true of them.

Two different kinds of item share this format, and they need different work. Sometimes A, B and C are number or algebra expressions, and you work each one out. Sometimes they are figures — whole shapes, or parts of one shape. Then the choices compare lengths, angles, areas, shaded parts or the number of sides and corners. Both appear on every form of the test.

Evaluate all three quantities before you read the choices, and write the three values down. Reading the choices first is the biggest time sink on this question type: you end up checking four statements against numbers you have not worked out yet, which means computing the same thing three or four times over. Three values first, then one pass through the choices.
Type one: comparing expressions

items: Work out A completely. Write the number down next to the letter.
Do the same for B, then for C. Do not skip one because it looks obviously biggest.
Put all three in the same form before you compare. All decimals, or all fractions over the same denominator — never a mixture.
Now read the choices, one at a time, and test each against your three numbers.
If a choice makes two claims joined by and, check both halves. The choice is wrong if either half is wrong.

blocks.text: Putting everything in one form is worth the two seconds it costs. \(\frac{3}{8}\), \(0.4\) and \(35\%\) are hard to rank while they are wearing different clothes and trivial once they are \(0.375\), \(0.4\) and \(0.35\). Decimals are usually the fastest common form, because you can compare them left to right one digit at a time.

blocks.stem: Examine A, B and C and choose the best answer.   A. \(25\%\) of \(88\)   B. \(\frac{1}{3}\) of \(63\)   C. \(0.4 \times 55\)
blocks.walkthrough: Evaluate before you read anything else. A is a quarter of 88, which is \(22\). B is a third of 63, which is \(21\). C is \(0.4 \times 55\), which is \(22\). Write down \(22\), \(21\), \(22\) and only now look at the choices: A and C are equal and both beat B, so the last choice is the one. Notice the second choice — it is half right, because A really is greater than B, but \(B = C\) is false, and a statement joined by and needs both halves to hold.

blocks.stem: Examine A, B and C and choose the best answer.   A. \(3 + 4 \times 5\)   B. \((3 + 4) \times 5\)   C. \(3 \times 4 + 5\)
blocks.walkthrough: These are the same three numbers in three arrangements, so the item is really about order of operations. A multiplies first: \(4 \times 5 = 20\), then \(3 + 20 = 23\). B has parentheses, so \(3 + 4 = 7\) first, then \(7 \times 5 = 35\). C multiplies first again: \(3 \times 4 = 12\), then \(12 + 5 = 17\). That gives \(35 \gt 23 \gt 17\), which is B, A, C. The trap is working A from left to right, getting \(35\), and concluding that A and B are equal.

blocks.stem: Examine A, B and C and choose the best answer.   A. \(\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2\)   B. \(\sqrt{\frac{9}{16}}\)   C. \(\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{4}{3}\)
blocks.walkthrough: A is \(\frac{9}{16}\), or \(0.5625\). B is the square root of \(\frac{9}{16}\), which is \(\frac{3}{4}\), or \(0.75\). C is a number multiplied by its own reciprocal, which is always \(1\). So C is largest, then B, then A. The point worth keeping is what happened to \(\frac{3}{4}\): squaring made it smaller and taking the root made it larger, because it sits between zero and one. Anyone who assumes squaring always grows a number picks the first choice.

blocks.text: Type two: comparing figures

Figures on the HSPT are not necessarily drawn to scale. A line that looks longer may not be. An angle that looks square may be \(80^\circ\). Two shaded regions that look equal may not be. Reason only from what the figure states — labeled measurements, tick marks, right-angle boxes, the words square or equilateral — and never from what the picture looks like.

That rule is the whole question type. The figures are drawn imprecisely on purpose, because the item is testing whether you know that a square's diagonal is longer than its side, not whether you can eyeball a drawing. If a statement cannot be settled from the stated properties, it is not the answer, however true it looks.

items: List what you are actually told. Side lengths, angle measures, the name of the shape, any marks showing that parts are equal.
Derive what follows. If two angles of a triangle are given, the third is \(180^\circ\) minus their sum. If a square's perimeter is given, its side is a quarter of it.
Write the derived numbers down. Do not carry them in your head while reading four statements.
Test each choice against those numbers, and reject any choice that depends on how the drawing looks.
If a figure is missing a measurement you would need, the honest answer may be that the two cannot be compared. Check whether a choice says so.

blocks.text: Because this page cannot show you a drawing, the two examples below describe the figures in words. That is useful practice in itself: the first thing to do with a figure on the test is translate it into a short list of stated facts, which is exactly what these stems already are.

blocks.stem: In triangle \(DEF\), angle \(D\) measures \(40^\circ\) and angle \(E\) measures \(95^\circ\). Choose the best answer.
options: \(\angle F\) is the largest angle in the triangle.
\(\angle D + \angle F\) is greater than \(\angle E\).
\(\angle D\), \(\angle E\) and \(\angle F\) are all equal.
blocks.walkthrough: Derive the missing angle first: the three angles of any triangle add to \(180^\circ\), so \(\angle F = 180 - 40 - 95 = 45^\circ\). Now your three numbers are \(40\), \(95\) and \(45\). The third choice is true, since \(45 \gt 40\). The first is false because \(\angle E\) is the largest. The second misses by ten degrees — \(40 + 45 = 85\), which is less than \(95\) — and it is the choice most students accept without computing, because two angles sounds like more than one.

blocks.stem: Square \(A\) has a perimeter of \(24\) cm. Rectangle \(B\) is \(8\) cm long and \(4\) cm wide. Circle \(C\) has a radius of \(4\) cm. Choose the best answer.
options: The area of \(A\) is less than the area of \(B\).
\(A\) and \(B\) have equal perimeters, but \(A\) has the greater area.
\(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) all have the same area.
blocks.walkthrough: Turn every figure into numbers before comparing anything. Square A has side \(24 \div 4 = 6\), so its area is \(36\) and its perimeter is \(24\). Rectangle B has area \(8 \times 4 = 32\) and perimeter \(2(8) + 2(4) = 24\). Circle C has area \(\pi \times 4^2 = 16\pi\), which is about \(50.3\). Both halves of the second choice hold: the perimeters match at \(24\), and \(36 \gt 32\). The third choice is the trap for anyone weighing a radius of \(4\) against a side of \(6\) by eye — the circle is in fact the largest of the three in area.

blocks.text: The facts these questions lean on

head: Situation
What is true
rows: \(x^3 \lt x^2 \lt x \lt \sqrt{x}\). Squaring shrinks it; taking a root grows it.
Area \(s^2\); perimeter \(4s\); the diagonal is longer than a side.
Area \(\frac{1}{2}bh\); the three angles add to \(180^\circ\); the longest side lies opposite the largest angle.
Six faces, 12 edges, eight vertices; volume \(s^3\); surface area \(6s^2\).
Do not mean equal areas. Of all rectangles with a given perimeter, the square encloses the most area.
Doubles the perimeter but multiplies the area by four.

blocks.text: The traps

items: A statement that is true but is not the best answer. The instruction says best for a reason. When two choices both look right, one of them is usually true of only part of the figure, or true only if the drawing is accurate. Prefer the one that follows from the stated facts alone.
A compound choice where only one half holds. Anything joined by and contains two claims and both must be true. Check the half you are less sure of first.
Judging shaded area by eye. If a choice compares shaded regions, count the equal parts the figure is divided into. If nothing tells you the parts are equal, you cannot compare them.

Forgetting what squaring does below one. \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}\), which is smaller. This is the most reliable trap in the section, and it covers \(0.3^2 = 0.09\) and \(0.9^2 = 0.81\) as well.
Comparing unlike measurements. If one quantity is a perimeter and another is an area, ranking them means nothing. Read what each letter measures before you order them.
Assuming a right angle. Unless the little square is drawn or the problem says so, an angle that looks like \(90^\circ\) is just an angle.

blocks.text: When you are stuck

items: Estimate. You rarely need exact values to rank three quantities. \(\frac{7}{15}\) is a shade under a half, and \(48\%\) of \(610\) is close to \(300\). Ranking is easier than computing.
Eliminate on one letter. If you are certain A is the largest, cross out every choice that puts anything above A. Two choices usually go at once.
Look for the equals sign. Test writers like items in which two of the three come out the same. If a quick look suggests two of your values match, check the choice containing \(=\) first.

Guess and move on. There is no penalty for a wrong answer on the HSPT, so mark your best remaining choice and go. A comparison you have half-solved still gives you a one-in-two guess, which is a fine trade for 30 seconds.

blocks.text: Worth memorizing

items: The fraction, decimal and percent table above. Knowing \(\frac{3}{8} = 0.375\) on sight saves you the long division every time.
Area and perimeter for the square, rectangle, triangle and circle.
A cube has six faces, 12 edges and eight vertices.
Between zero and one, squaring makes a number smaller and a square root makes it bigger. Above one, the reverse.
Evaluate first, read the choices second. That is a habit rather than a fact, and it is worth more than any of the formulas.

Geometric Comparison.title: Geometric Comparison
Geometric Comparison.weight: About six of the 52 Quantitative Skills questions
Geometric Comparison.oneLine: Three labeled figures are compared on area, perimeter, angle measure or length, and you pick the two-part statement that is true of all three.

blocks.text: A geometric comparison shows you three small drawings labeled \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) with their measurements printed on them. The four choices are not numbers. Each one is a compound statement such as The area of \(A\) equals the area of \(C\), and the area of \(B\) is greater than the area of \(A\), and exactly one of them is true of all three figures.

Four things get compared, and the stem always says which: area, perimeter or distance around, the measure of an angle marked \(x\), or the length of a labeled segment. Read that word first. A student who computes three areas for a question that asked about perimeters has done all the work and still cannot answer, and the choices are written so that the area ordering is a different ordering from the perimeter ordering.
The method

items: Read the stem and name the measure. Area, perimeter, angle or length. Write that word at the top of your scratch space.
Copy the labeled numbers off each figure. Side lengths, the two given angles, the radius — whatever is actually printed.
Compute all three values before you look at a single choice. Write \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) down the page with a number beside each.
Rank your three numbers and say the ordering to yourself: they are all equal, or two match and one is bigger, or they run \(A\), \(C\), \(B\).
Now read the choices once. Each has two clauses joined by and. Test the clauses separately and reject the choice the moment either clause fails.
If two choices survive, you have made an arithmetic slip somewhere. Recompute the value that appears in both.

blocks.text: Compute all three before the choices, every time. If you read the choices first you end up computing the area of \(A\) once for each choice that mentions it, which is four times the work in a section that gives you 35 seconds a question. Three numbers, then one pass down the list.
Read the labels, not the picture

The drawings are not to scale and are frequently drawn to mislead. In one item on this site figure \(B\) is a rectangle 10 cm by 2 cm, easily the widest of the three on the page, and it has the smallest area of the three. In another, figure \(C\) is a square 5 cm on a side that looks smaller across than a rectangle 8 cm by 3 cm, and it is the largest. Width is not area. Height is not perimeter. Nothing you can see with your eye is evidence.

The same goes the other way. If a figure is called a square, every side is equal even when the drawing looks oblong. If a triangle is called equilateral, all three sides match the one number printed on it. If a right-angle box is drawn, the angle is \(90^\circ\); if no box is drawn, an angle that looks square is just an angle. Work from the words and the numbers only.
The formulas you need
The whole question type runs on six formulas and four angle totals. There is nothing else to learn, so learn these to the point where you are not deriving them under time pressure.

head: Figure
Area
Distance around
rows: split it into rectangles and add

blocks.stem: Figure \(A\) is a rectangle 6 cm by 4 cm, figure \(B\) is a rectangle 8 cm by 3 cm and figure \(C\) is a square 5 cm on each side. Compare the areas and choose the best answer.
options: The area of \(A\) equals the area of \(B\), and the area of \(C\) equals the area of \(A\).
The area of \(A\) equals the area of \(B\), and the area of \(C\) is greater than the area of \(A\).
The area of \(A\) is greater than the area of \(B\), and the area of \(B\) is greater than the area of \(C\).
The area of \(A\) equals the area of \(B\), and the area of \(C\) is less than the area of \(A\).
blocks.walkthrough: Three numbers first. \(A\) is \(6 \times 4 = 24\), \(B\) is \(8 \times 3 = 24\) and \(C\) is \(5 \times 5 = 25\), all in square centimeters. So \(A\) and \(B\) match and \(C\) beats both by one. Now down the choices: the second is the only one whose two clauses both hold. The last choice is the trap, and it is a trap about the drawing rather than the arithmetic — \(C\) is the shortest figure across the page, so it looks like the small one, and it is the biggest by a single square centimeter.

blocks.text: Triangles and composite figures

Two figures cause almost all the arithmetic errors in this question type. The first is the triangle: its area is half the base times the height, and forgetting the half turns a triangle of area 36 into one of area 72, which is enough to reverse the whole ordering. The second is the composite figure, usually an L shape. Cut it into two rectangles, find each area and add them. Treating an L shape as the full rectangle it sits inside inflates the area by the piece that was cut out, and the choices are built to reward exactly that mistake.

blocks.stem: Figure \(A\) is a square 6 cm on each side, figure \(B\) is a rectangle 9 cm by 4 cm and figure \(C\) is a right triangle with legs of 12 cm and 6 cm. Compare the areas and choose the best answer.
options: The area of \(A\) is greater than the area of \(B\), and the area of \(B\) is greater than the area of \(C\).
The area of \(A\) equals the area of \(B\), and the area of \(B\) equals the area of \(C\).
The area of \(A\) equals the area of \(B\), and the area of \(C\) is greater than the area of \(B\).
The area of \(A\) equals the area of \(B\), and the area of \(C\) is less than the area of \(B\).
blocks.walkthrough: \(A\) is \(6 \times 6 = 36\). \(B\) is \(9 \times 4 = 36\). \(C\) is \(\frac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 6 = 36\). All three are 36 square centimeters, so the second choice is right and the item is testing one thing only. Skip the half on the triangle and you get 72, which makes \(C\) the largest and sends you to the third choice — the choice that is there for precisely that slip. When a figure is a triangle, halve before you compare.

blocks.text: Area and perimeter are independent

This is the fact the question type is built on, and it is worth stating flatly: a figure with a larger area can have a smaller perimeter. A square 6 cm on a side has area 36 and perimeter 24. A rectangle 12 cm by 2 cm has area 24 and perimeter 28. The square has the bigger area and the shorter distance around, and if you rank one measure by looking at the other you will be wrong.

Two more consequences follow. Equal perimeters do not mean equal areas: rectangles 7 cm by 3 cm, 5 cm by 5 cm and 8 cm by 2 cm all have a perimeter of 20 cm and areas of 21, 25 and 16 square centimeters. And equal areas do not mean equal perimeters: a square 6 cm on a side and a rectangle 9 cm by 4 cm both cover 36 square centimeters, but the perimeters are 24 cm and 26 cm. Of all rectangles holding a given area, the square has the shortest perimeter, and the more stretched the rectangle the more edge it needs.

blocks.stem: Figure \(A\) is a square 6 cm on each side, figure \(B\) is a rectangle 12 cm by 2 cm and figure \(C\) is a rectangle 9 cm by 4 cm. Compare the perimeters and choose the best answer.
options: The perimeter of \(B\) is less than the perimeter of \(C\), and the perimeter of \(C\) is less than the perimeter of \(A\).
The perimeter of \(A\) is less than the perimeter of \(C\), and the perimeter of \(C\) is less than the perimeter of \(B\).
The perimeter of \(A\) equals the perimeter of \(C\), and the perimeter of \(B\) is greater than the perimeter of \(A\).
The perimeter of \(A\) is greater than the perimeter of \(C\), and the perimeter of \(C\) is greater than the perimeter of \(B\).
blocks.walkthrough: The stem says perimeters, so add the sides and leave the areas alone. \(A\) is \(4 \times 6 = 24\) cm, \(B\) is \(2(12) + 2(2) = 28\) cm and \(C\) is \(2(9) + 2(4) = 26\) cm, giving \(A\) less than \(C\) less than \(B\). Notice what the areas would have told you: 36, 24 and 36 square centimeters. \(A\) and \(C\) cover the same ground and need different amounts of fence, and \(B\) has the smallest area with the longest perimeter. Anyone who ranks this item by area gets a tie at the top and no matching choice.

blocks.text: Angles

Angle items give you two of the angles in each figure and mark the third with an \(x\). The only question is what the angles in that figure add to, and there are three answers: a triangle totals \(180^\circ\), angles filling a straight line total \(180^\circ\), and angles filling the space around a point total \(360^\circ\). Subtract the two given angles from the right total and you have \(x\). Using \(180^\circ\) where the figure needs \(360^\circ\) produces negative angles, which is your signal that you picked the wrong total rather than that the item is broken.
